q: You see a crew member fall over the side. What do you do first?
a: Shout 'Man overboard!' and point at them
o: Jump in after them straight away
Go below to wake the skipper
Start the engine before anything else
why: Raise the alarm and keep them in sight — a head in the waves is very easy to lose.

q: The skipper makes you the spotter while the boat turns back. What is your job?
a: Point at the person and never look away
o: Point once, then help with the sheets
Fetch the first-aid kit from below
Call the coastguard on the VHF
why: The spotter keeps eyes and an arm on the casualty until they are back alongside.

fig.note: Skipper turning the boat to come back

q: Seconds after the shout of 'Man overboard!', you are next to the lifebuoy and danbuoy at the stern. What do you do?
a: Throw them out towards the person at once
o: Keep them aboard until the boat turns back
Throw them only once the person is close
Wait for the skipper to tell you to throw
why: Thrown at once, they give the casualty something to hold and mark the spot.

q: Why do you press the MOB button on the plotter now?
a: It marks the spot so you can steer back to it
o: It stops the engine and the propeller
It sounds the horn to warn other boats
It switches on all the deck lights
why: The plotter saves the position where the person went in and shows the way back.

fig.title: Chart plotter
lines: Big red MOB button on the screen

q: A pan of cooking oil catches fire on the stove. What do you do?
a: Turn off the gas and cover it with the fire blanket
o: Throw a cup of water over the flames
Carry the pan out to the cockpit
Spray it with the cockpit hose
why: Smother a fat fire; water makes burning oil erupt out of the pan.

q: Spilt diesel is burning in the bilge under the engine. Which do you reach for?
a: A powder extinguisher, aimed at the base
o: A bucket of seawater thrown over it
The deck wash hose on full
A towel to fan the flames down
why: Never water on a fuel fire — it spreads the burning fuel. Use powder, CO2 or foam.

q: A candle has set a bunk cushion smouldering in the forward cabin. Your friend says 'never use water on a boat fire'. Is she right here?
a: No — water is fine on burning fabric
o: Yes — water is never used below decks
Yes — only powder works on cushions
Yes — water makes any fire spread
why: Water suits solids such as fabric and wood; keep it off burning fat, fuel and wiring.

q: You go below and find this. What do you do first?
a: Tell the skipper, then help find where it comes in
o: Bail quietly so as not to worry anyone
Lift your bags onto the bunks to keep them dry
Call MAYDAY on the VHF straight away
why: The skipper must know at once; finding the source matters more than pumping.

fig.title: Below, under sail
lines: Skipper on deck at the helm

q: Water is rising slowly in the bilge. You taste it: fresh, not salty. What does that suggest?
a: A leak from the fresh water tank or its pipes
o: A hole in the hull below the waterline
A failed toilet seacock letting the sea in
Waves coming in through the cockpit drains
why: Fresh water means the boat's own system is leaking, not the sea coming in.

q: The skipper is hurt and cannot use the radio; you must send a MAYDAY by voice. How do you set the VHF?
a: Channel 16, high power
o: Channel 16, low power
Channel 70, high power
The marina's working channel
why: Distress voice calls go on channel 16, at full power for the best range.

q: Under a flap on the VHF you find a red button marked DISTRESS. What does pressing and holding it do?
a: Sends an automatic alert with the boat's ID and position
o: Calls the nearest marina on its own channel
Locks the radio on channel 16 for listening
Turns on the strobe light at the masthead
why: The DSC distress button sends a digital MAYDAY alert, with the GPS position if one is connected.

q: After 'MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, this is yacht ORCA…', what do you say?
a: Position, what is wrong, help needed, people aboard
o: Your names, home port and next harbour
The boat's name again, until someone answers
The time, the weather and the sea state
why: Where you are comes first, then the problem, the help you need and how many are aboard.

q: How do you look after this crew member?
a: Shelter, dry clothes, blankets, a warm sweet drink
o: A hot shower straight away and a brandy
Rub their arms and legs hard to warm them
Leave them in wet clothes in the wind to dry
why: Warm them gently: out of the wind, dry layers, a warm drink if alert — never alcohol.

q: Boiling water from the kettle spills over a crew member's forearm. What do you do?
a: Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes
o: Spread butter or oil on it at once
Pop the blisters so the skin can dry
Hold ice straight against the skin
why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the burn; then cover it loosely with cling film.

q: How do you look after Anna?
a: Keep her still, watch her and tell the skipper now
o: Let her sleep it off alone in her bunk
Give her painkillers and a cold beer
Put her on the helm to keep her busy
why: Confusion after a blow to the head is a sign of serious injury — she needs watching and medical advice.

fig.title: Accidental gybe
lines: The boom hit Anna on the side of the head
Later: confused, asking the same thing

q: How do you help your friend?
a: Keep giving small sips and tell the skipper
o: Let her sleep — seasickness passes on its own
Give her a large glass of water in one go
Give her strong coffee to perk her up
why: Long seasickness dehydrates: small frequent sips, and the skipper may need to get medical advice.

fig.title: Day two of a rough passage
lines: Your friend has been sick for 12 hours
Weak, dizzy, passing very little urine

q: What do you do for the helmsman?
a: Shade, lie down, cool with water, sip fluids
o: Strong coffee, then back to the helm
Keep steering — it will pass by evening
Move into full sun to sweat it out
why: Heat exhaustion: get them cool and shaded and give fluids before it turns into heatstroke.

q: A crew member collapses in the saloon. They are unconscious but breathing normally. How do you lay them while you wait for help?
a: On their side, in the recovery position
o: Flat on their back, head on a pillow
Sitting up, propped against a bunk
Face down, arms by their sides
why: On their side the airway stays open and any vomit can drain out.

q: A guest wants to get into the raft right now. When do you get in?
a: When the yacht is going down — step up into it
o: Now — a liferaft is always the safer place
Now, by jumping down into it from the deck
Once you have swum across to it
why: Stay aboard as long as you can: you should step up into the raft as the yacht sinks.

fig.title: Abandon ship?
lines: Yacht still afloat, water rising slowly

q: In what order do you act?
a: Shout, throw the buoys, press MOB, guest points
o: Press MOB, call MAYDAY, then throw the buoys
Call MAYDAY, then shout, then throw the buoys
Turn the boat, then shout, throw the buoys
why: Alarm, something to float on and a marked position come first — then the radio call.

fig.title: Night, sailing, F4
lines: The skipper falls over the side
Only you and one guest aboard
